The speed edge over xoshiro256** is only about 1.2x and seiran128 ties sfc64 (1.21), so the clear wins are over the reference MT19937-64 C code and PCG64 only; std::mt19937_64 was not timed. The author says that, being new, it has not been investigated by others. The PractRand 32 TB, BigCrush, gjrand and hwd results are the author's own. Not cryptographic: the author recovered the full state from 3 consecutive outputs with Z3 in a few minutes. seiran128.c uses a global static state and exports bare next()/init() symbols, so it must be wrapped before use as a library. CC0 dedication gives no patent grant. The last commit (2021) only added a C# port.

It relies on arithmetic right shift of a negative int64_t (the README says 'MUST use arithmetic right shift'), which is implementation-defined in C before C23 and in C++ before C++20. It uses a global static state with bare next()/init() symbols. CC0 dedication gives no patent grant. Four commits, the last on 2019-08-18. It is a sibling of seiran128 (same author, same table).

corrections.claimed_speedup: README (Travis CI run, 2020-05-18): BM_IRNG_next 2.32 ns and BM_FRNG_next 2.31 ns per value. The author's scalar reference of the same recurrence (BM_reference_next 3.45 ns, BM_reference_nextFloat 3.75 ns) is about 1.49x and 1.62x slower. BM_mt19937 6.33 ns and BM_uniform_real_distribution<float> 6.84 ns are about 2.7x and 3.0x slower. All ratios are derived from page data. The std::mt19937 comparison does not produce the same outputs: the library and its reference use upper mask 0x8000000, not MT19937's 0x80000000, so they do not compute MT19937. The work per value is the same, though.
corrections.baseline: std::mt19937 and std::uniform_real_distribution<float> (libstdc++ via g++-7), POSIX random/lrand48/drand48, and the author's scalar reference (test/src/reference.hpp, a competitive-programming MT variant with the same non-standard mask)
corrections.caveats: CORRECTNESS: this is not MT19937. include/mt.hpp generate() (and its scalar reference test/src/reference.hpp) computes y = (MT[i] & 0x8000000UL) + (MT[i+NS] & 0x7FFFFFFFUL), masking bit 27 instead of MT19937's upper bit 0x80000000 and combining with '+', so carries make the recurrence non-linear. The MT19937 period and equidistribution guarantees therefore do not apply. A Python re-implementation (seed 1) differs from true MT19937 from the 2nd output on (1847 of the first 2000 values differ), and the true-MT check value 4123659995 was confirmed. The SIMD path does match its scalar reference: gtest compares 8 streams x 20000 values. So the 1.49x win over the reference is like-for-like, while the 2.7x win over std::mt19937 compares different generators of equal cost. Fixing the mask should not change speed, but this was not measured. The output is 8 interleaved streams seeded seed..seed+7, not a single MT19937 sequence. FRNG computes (y+0.5f)/2^32 in float, which rounds to exactly 1.0f for the top 128 values of y, so its range is [0,1] rather than [0,1). next(a,b) uses modulo and is biased. The numbers come from a first-party run on a shared CI VM with no CPU model; the author notes a smaller edge over the reference on his laptop ('your mileage may vary'). 0 stars; last commit 2020-05-18.

notes: A same-generator check was done as asked. The SIMD path equals its scalar reference, but both carry the 0x8000000 mask typo (also found in a common competitive-programming RNG template), so the 'Mersenne Twister' timed against std::mt19937 is a different, non-linear generator. Unlike SIMDxorshift, the bug does not reduce work per output, so I kept the entry with the correctness bug recorded. Reject instead if the SIMDxorshift/stb-zip precedent is read as 'computes a different function than the named baseline'.
